current_episode.title: From Sports Psychology to Cybersecurity: Building a Business Through Adaptation (Bryant Wallace, Founder/CEO, WallScott Solutions)

guest.bio_context: Bryant Wallace started his entrepreneurial journey at age nine working in his cousin's health food store called Greatest Grains. He attended the University of Northern Iowa where he studied sports psychology and education. He founded WallScott Solutions in 1999 after graduating in 1996, and has been running the same business for 27 years, specializing in cybersecurity and compliance services while applying sports psychology principles to business coaching.

context.real_quote: I can go fast by myself or I can go further with others, and now I can go further faster with the right others.

context.transcript_excerpt: Welcome to the Think Small Podcast, hyper growth for small businesses. So, what's slowing you down? Hi, this is Gene Bohensky with the Think Small Podcast. And here we've got another exciting episode. We have Bryant Wallace from Walscott Solutions. The company focuses on cybersecurity and compliance for a wide range of industries. And Bryant has some interesting things that he's learned in his career and a couple of unique approaches to business that he'd like to share with us. So thanks, Brian, for agreeing to do the podcast. Well, thank you, Gene. Thank you for having me. I really do appreciate the opportunity. I'm excited for this conversation. So to get started, tell me a little bit about your background, how you got started in business as an entrepreneur. I think you started really young, right? And how that led to you starting your IT company. Yes, I did. I started very young. I started at nine years old. And at the time, my cousin had started a health food store. It was called Greatest Grains. And I wanted the opportunity to just dock the shelves, bag the groceries, because I thought it was a way for me to make a few dollars, a dollar an hour. And I begged and pleaded, and I had the opportunity to work for my cousin at his health food store. And in that process, it really began to open my eyes to the possibilities. So I knew that I wanted to be an entrepreneur. I just wasn't sure what industry or how we're going to go about doing so. But it did teach me how to talk to people from all over the world, different languages, different cultures. And again, it was able to expand my imagination of possibilities. I mean, I always find that people, when they're exposed to entrepreneurship early in life that really sets them on the course for the rest of their life, right? Yes. And actually, I think I was even an early problem solver because I just wanted to have an extra quarter to buy an extra chocolate milk at lunch. That was my hardship, was how to buy an extra chocolate milk. Well, a lot of times it's those simple things that drive people to do more and figure out how to get things that they wouldn't otherwise get, right? I mean, that's one of the prime motivations for starting your own business is I want my freedom, I want to earn more, and I want to achieve more, right? Right, right. And also just really to have that flexibility. Because while he owned a grocery store and his family, he would still take us around to different events in the community. He actually would drive us from Iowa, is where I grew up, and he would take us to Chicago, Let us see what the Museum of Science and Industry and just see Chicago coming from a small town, Davenport, Iowa. And for him to have that flexibility, that's what I wanted. I wanted to be able to have that freedom of not just working, but then also being able to do these really cool things to be able to travel around and just see. So I thought that he was, I just thought he was so rich to be able to do that and give us a chance to then buy a chocolate milk, but also then give us lunch and give us an education about just the possibilities of life. Right. So in our earlier conversations, you really talked about being an athlete and how being an athlete has shaped your approach to business. Maybe you want to explain about that, how you got into sports and becoming an athlete and how that crosses over to business. Right. And I'll tell you, while going to junior high and high school, I did play sports. I would call myself an athlete. I was there. I was participating. I may not have been the best, but I really did want to work hard. I understood what it meant to work hard and then see your results. and I knew that I wanted to go to college. And in the process of thinking about where I wanted to go, it also gonna be what my major And what I found was the gym teacher at my high school he had the best job ever All day he just made sure that we could play sports He also just really encouraged us

pending_qa.q: What major technology shifts has a cybersecurity firm had to help clients adapt to over the past 25 years?
pending_qa.r: Since starting in 1999, WallScott Solutions has helped businesses navigate Y2K preparedness, the emergence of social media and digital profile risks, compliance adoption, and now AI implementation. Wallace emphasizes that while technology continues to change, the core focus remains on bringing the human element into business operations, particularly through customer service and relationships.

pending_qa.q: How should business leaders balance automation and AI implementation with maintaining human relationships and customer service?
pending_qa.r: Wallace argues that while automation and AI can make businesses run more efficiently, the number one thing needed in business is sales, which comes through customer service and relationships. The challenge is to automate certain processes while keeping the human element central to the business strategy. This requires understanding threats and vulnerabilities while maintaining focus on good customer service.

pending_qa.q: What role do small business owners play in developing their communities and what responsibility do they have?
pending_qa.r: Wallace views entrepreneurs and business owners as critical components of their communities, not just for providing goods and services but for developing the community. He emphasizes that many people have their first jobs at small local shops. He has shifted from thinking about 'giving back' to seeing business owners as continual contributors to their communities through hiring, internships, and nonprofit board service.
